title: Alternatives when tuning is discontinued and total cost of ownership

opening.headline: When your provider doesn't offer or limits tuning, learn how to compare the path to achieving your goals without tuning versus the total cost of ownership.
body: Plans that rely on tuning are exposed to changes in provider policy. The Gemini API does not have models that support tuning, tuning is provided by the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and OpenAI's fine-tuning platform is also inaccessible to new users. If you don't want your plan to fall apart when tuning gets stuck, you need to have an alternative route.

In this class, you'll explore alternative paths using a combination of state-of-the-art models, prompts, and searches, and learn how to compare them based on total cost of ownership, which consists of startup costs, operating costs, conversion costs, and risk costs. Next, the instructor explains cases where tuning cannot be used in the Gemini API and cases where switching points are determined.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Tuning models and latest base model/prompt combinations can be distinguished by total cost of ownership.
Can judge the feasibility of alternative routes

screens.title: What happens to our plans if our provider stops tuning?
screens.lead: Read the situation of a team that made a plan based on tuning. It's helpful to think about which parts of your plan are weak.

paragraphs: While one team was creating a service using the Gemini API, they planned to improve response consistency through tuning later. However, Gemini API and AI Studio no longer support models for fine-tuning, and tuning is supported in the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

The situation is similar for other providers. OpenAI's fine-tuning platform is not accessible to new users, and only eligible existing customers can create training jobs. Plans that rely on tuning like this are subject to changes in provider policy.
If so, your plan will be solid if there is a way to reach the same goal without tuning. This class covers how to find the way and compare tuning paths by the same criteria.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Tuning is not a last resort, but one of several paths. Being able to compare routes makes your choices rationale.

screens.outro: First, let's think of a method that can be used without tuning.

screens.title: Think About It: How to Achieve Your Goals Without Tuning
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so come up with it yourself first and then click on it.

items.prompt: Is there a way to increase response consistency without tuning?
items.answer: The first thing to try is improving your prompts by making your instructions clear and direct and adding a few examples. By explicitly requesting the desired behavior, your model takes less guessing from vague instructions.

items.prompt: How can we give the model information it doesn’t know?
items.answer: There is a way to find the information you need through search and put it into context. For facts that the model does not know, old knowledge, and in-house information, search is an appropriate solution rather than tuning.

items.prompt: What if we change to a better model?
items.answer: There are cases where a new model catches up to the effect achieved by tuning on an older model with just a prompt. Before planning tuning, it is best to first measure with the same evaluation set on the latest model.

screens.outro: Let's look specifically at an alternative path that ties these three together.

screens.title: Alternative Path: Latest Model, Prompt, Search
screens.lead: Select each tab to see which problems can be solved by alternative paths to tuning.

tabs.label: two axes
tabs.body: Optimization is not a linear sequence but rather a lever to solve different problems. Contextual optimization increases response accuracy when the model is unaware of the information, when the knowledge is outdated, or when in-house information is needed. Model optimization increases consistency of behavior when formatting, tone, or reasoning are inconsistent. You need to first figure out which axis the problem lies on so you can pull the right lever.

tabs.label: prompt
tabs.body: Improving prompts is the first step in establishing a baseline, and is often sufficient for tasks such as summarization, translation, and code generation. Making your instructions clear and direct, clearly requesting the desired behavior, structuring it (e.g. separated by XML tags), and providing several examples will increase accuracy and consistency.

tabs.label: Search (RAG)
tabs.body: When the knowledge base is large, RAG is used to search for the necessary pieces and paste them into the prompt. When a traditional RAG is divided into pieces, the context is lost and search may fail. Contextual Retrieval is a method of reducing retrieval failures by adding context to each fragment, responding to the problem of context being lost when documents are truncated. If your knowledge base is smaller than 200,000 tokens, you can also put the entire knowledge base into a prompt. As scale increases, search becomes a more scalable choice. When choosing a search path, we separately check whether the information required for search is actually found using the evaluation set.

tabs.label: latest model
tabs.body: Sometimes new models come close to previous tuning models with just a prompt. Changing models has lower setup costs compared to tuning. However, as the model changes, the behavior also changes, so you need to check it again by measuring it with the same evaluation set.

screens.outro: Now that we have the routes sorted out, let’s see how they compare in terms of total cost of ownership.

screens.title: Total cost of ownership comparison table for both routes
screens.lead: Compare the costs of the tuning path and the prompt/search path across four items in the table. For each item, take a look at which one is more burdensome.

data.caption: Total cost of ownership compared to tuning path and prompt/search path
rows: There are costs first for data preparation and training.
There are costs involved in designing prompts, constructing assessment sets, and organizing searches.
There are invocation costs and maintenance costs such as evaluation, retraining, and data management.
The token cost per call can be high due to long prompts and retrieved context.
If the underlying model changes, it must be retrained and evaluated.
As the model changes, re-adjust and evaluate the prompts.
Exposure to provider policy changes or model termination.
There is a risk that model behavior will change. We detect this with the evaluation set.
data.notes: Total cost of ownership is the total cost from introduction, operation, conversion, and risk. Before comparing costs, you must first measure the quality of both paths using the same success criteria and the same evaluation set. If the quality is similar, it is judged by cost, and if the quality is different, it is judged by adding the value of the quality. If you compare costs without measuring quality, the cheaper route may produce worse results. Additionally, each cell in the table will vary in size depending on call volume and your team's operational capabilities, so fill in the numbers for your situation and compare. Even for the same item, conclusions may be different for small and large services.

screens.outro: Now let's apply the alternative path as an example.

screens.title: Case Commentary: Alternative Paths When Gemini API Does Not Provide Tuning
screens.lead: The instructor explains a hypothetical case. Click the Next button to review alternative routes one by one.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The team creating services with the Gemini API has planned a tuning model. However, the API does not have a model that supports tuning. The question is whether the plan should be abandoned or if there is another way.

steps.title: Alternative 1: Tuning on platform
steps.body: The Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform allows you to tune Gemini models using supervised, reinforcement learning, and preference tuning. To achieve the same goal with tuning, you need to determine the cost of moving the product and the scope of model support. There are also restrictions such as region and API version.

steps.title: Alternative 2: Newer Model + Prompt
steps.body: The improved prompts and examples are applied to the latest model and measured using the same evaluation set. If the problem you're trying to solve with tuning is consistency, sometimes prompts and examples are all you need to get there.

steps.title: Alternative 3: Search
steps.body: If the cause of the problem is information the model does not know, tuning will not solve it. The right lever is to supply the necessary information in context through search (RAG).

steps.title: Compare and Choose
steps.body: Compare the total cost of ownership of the three alternatives in a table, but first measure the quality using the same evaluation set, leaving only the alternatives that reach the goal. Among the remaining alternatives, choose the one with the lower sum of initial, operating, transition, and risk costs.

screens.outro: This time, we will see when to decide whether to continue tuning or switch.

screens.title: Case Commentary: When to Decide Whether to Continue Tuning or Switch
screens.lead: The instructor explains the decision-making process for teams already running a tuning model. Click the Next button to see the decision-making process along the three axes.

steps.title: 1 Measure the gap
steps.body: Based on the evaluation set, we measure the quality gap between the path to improve prompts in the latest model and the current tuning model. This number is the starting point for all decisions.

steps.title: 2 When the gap is small
steps.body: If the gap is small and the cost of maintaining tuning is high, switch. This is because it reduces the evaluation, retraining, and data management costs of maintaining tuning.

steps.title: 3 When the gap is large
steps.body: If the gap is large and replacement is difficult, stay tuned. However, risk is reduced by establishing a shutdown schedule and retuning plan for the base model.

steps.title: 4 Decide on three axes
steps.body: The transition point is determined by three axes: gap, cost, and risk. If you only look at one axis, your judgment will be biased to one side. By organizing the three axes in one table, the team can discuss them on the same basis. In the table, write down the current value of each axis and the basis for judgment.

steps.title: See it as 5 options
steps.body: Tuning is not a last resort, but an option for comparison. If you win the comparison, you choose it, and if you lose, you don't use it. With this perspective, your plan will not change even if your provider's policies change. If you regularly re-measure the gap between the two paths using the same evaluation set, you can know in numbers at that time when a switch is necessary.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Key theorems and connections
screens.lead: We outline alternatives for tuning outages and the total cost of ownership. As you read, think of alternatives to our plan.

paragraphs: Tuning is not a last resort, but an option when comparing costs. An alternative is to combine prompts and searches in modern models, with different levers depending on whether the problem is contextual or behavioral.

Paths are compared by total cost of ownership. Combine initial costs, operating costs, conversion costs, and risk costs, but first compare quality using the same success criteria and the same evaluation set.

Whether to continue tuning or switch is determined by three axes: gap, cost, and risk. By having the evaluation set and success criteria independent of the model, any path can be compared using the same criteria.

Going back to the initial question, in order for the plan to not fall apart if the provider stops tuning, the quality and cost of the alternative routes must be evaluated in advance in the same evaluation set and in the same framework. That way, even if tuning is blocked, you can decide based on which path to move to.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The scope of tuning support provided by the provider varies by product and model. When making a plan, organize which products and methods can be used.

checks.intro: Think of the four components of total cost of ownership: Just pair the contents with the items in the tuning path.
checks.q: Match that with the total cost of ownership items in your tuning path.
right: Replacing the base model requires retraining
Exposure to changes in provider policy or model termination
Cost of data preparation and training
checks.explain: The tuning path has costs for initial data preparation and learning, operation, maintenance, relearning during transition, and risk exposure to policy changes.
checks.correctFeedback: All four cost items were matched correctly.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some things have changed. Re-pair them based on when the costs are incurred: when starting, operating, or changing.

checks.intro: Think about the criteria for deciding when to switch. You just have to choose the decision that best suits the situation.
checks.q: The quality of the latest model and improvement prompt is almost the same as the tuning model, and the tuning maintenance cost is large. How to judge correctly?
options: Tuning is a last resort, so always maintain it.
Since the gap is small and maintenance costs are high, we choose to switch.
Follow the established reputation of the tuning model without considering cost
Decide based on team preference without evaluation set
checks.explain: Measure the gap using the same evaluation set and switch if it is small and the tuning maintenance cost is high. If the gap is large and replacement is difficult, maintain tuning, but create a termination schedule and re-tuning plan.

wrong.0: Tuning is not a last resort, but rather an option when comparing costs.
wrong.2: The transition point is determined by three axes: gap, cost, and risk.
wrong.3: Quality must first be measured using the same evaluation set to provide a basis for judgment.

checks.correctFeedback: That's a good decision. If the gap is small and the maintenance costs are large, switching makes sense.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Read again to see what the two facts of this situation indicate: quality gap and maintenance cost.

glossary.def: This is the total cost including introduction, operation, transition, and risk.
This is a way to achieve the same goal without tuning.
It is an approach that combines the latest basic model with improved prompts and examples.
It is time to decide whether to abandon the current path and move to another path.

misconceptions.myth: Tuning is always the final solution.
misconceptions.fact: There is a separate problem that prompts and searches solve. First, distinguish whether the problem is contextual or behavioral.

misconceptions.myth: Alternative routes are of lower quality.
misconceptions.fact: You won't know until you measure it with the same evaluation set. In some cases, newer models and improvement prompts are closer to tuning.

misconceptions.myth: Total cost of ownership is the cost of learning.
misconceptions.fact: Includes operating, transition and risk costs. Learning costs are part of the initial cost.

closing.lead: The key points of this class are summarized as follows.
points: Tuning is one option when comparing costs.
Alternatives are Latest Models, Prompts, and Search.
Total cost of ownership is compared with quality based on the same evaluation set.
The timing of transition is determined by gaps, costs, and risks.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for you to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: If tuning is not available, how will our plan reach the same goal?
